query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A low‐temperature aging heat treatment that induces a homogeneous dispersion of coherent nanoscale L12 precipitates within the ductile FCC lamella can simultaneously increase yield strength and room‐temperature tensile ductility in eutectic dual‐phase high-entropy alloys by enhancing dislocation storage and retarding microcrack initiation at phase boundaries.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies (e.g., FCC and B2 phases) featuring semi-coherent phase boundaries that act as both dislocation sources and sites for microcrack initiation.
generation.intervention: Apply a low-temperature aging (annealing) treatment designed to precipitate fine, coherent L12 intermetallic particles preferentially within the FCC lamella without coarsening the existing lamellar structure.
generation.conditions: The treatment temperature and duration must be optimized (e.g., below 500°C for a controlled period) to induce nanoscale precipitation without altering the overall dual-phase lamellar morphology or triggering unwanted phase transformations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a uniform dispersion of coherent L12 precipitates within the FCC phase and along its nearby internal boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The coherent L12 precipitates serve as strong obstacles to dislocation motion, promoting dislocation accumulation and enhanced work hardening. They also help distribute local strains more evenly and prevent stress concentrations at the semi-coherent phase boundaries, thereby limiting microcrack initiation and propagation during tensile deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified lamellar baseline, the aged alloy will show an increased yield strength and higher uniform elongation at room temperature due to improved work hardening and reduced microcracking.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic alloy exhibits dual-phase lamellar colonies with semi-coherent boundaries that, while providing dislocation sources, also allow microcrack nucleation under tensile load, limiting ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects hinge on maintaining a nanoscale, coherent precipitate distribution. Overaging (leading to coarser precipitates or loss of interface coherence) or treatments that alter the lamellar morphology would not yield the improved mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of strength and ductility improvement depends on precise control of the aging parameters and the resulting precipitate size/distribution. It remains to be seen whether the enhancement in ductility might partially offset any potential rise in yield stress that could adversely affect deformation uniformity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical eutectic high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to the proposed low-temperature aging treatment to induce L12 precipitates and leave the other set as the unmodified control. Perform room-temperature tensile tests on both sets while conducting detailed microstructural characterization (TEM, STEM, and dislocation density mapping) to verify precipitate formation and distribution.
measurements: Tensile stress-strain response (to assess yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and uniform elongation)
TEM/STEM imaging to confirm the presence, size, and dispersion of the L12 precipitates
Quantification of dislocation densities and mapping of microcrack initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aging treatment does not lead to a statistically significant increase in both yield strength and tensile ductility relative to the control, or if the expected nanoscale coherent L12 precipitates are not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The properties of many metallic alloys are essentially related to the structure, morphology and chemical distribution of boundaries. In terms of atomic structure, the phase boundaries contained in eutectic dual-phase HEAs were supposed to be insufficient in prohibiting dislocations due to their semi-coherent nature, which is similar to those widely reported in NiAl dual-phase intermetallic alloys,. However, in-situ deformation tests revealed that dense dislocation storage can be achieved within FCC phases and dislocation walls were formed along phase boundaries. The unexpected strong interfaces are thought to be highly related to the chemically disordered distribution of multiple solution atoms at phase boundaries as well as in the matrix of HEAs. Particularly, an ultra-thin segregation zone of randomly distributed Cr atoms, typically less than 2 nm in width (Fig. 3b and S4), was detected near the phase boundary without forming complex intermetallic compounds, which were intrinsically brittle and would lead to stress concentration. Recent studies indicate that eutectic high-entropy alloys can simultaneously possess high strength and high ductility, which have potential industrial applications. The present study focuses on Al0.7CoCrFeNi, a lamellar dual-phase (fcc + B2) precipitation-strengthenable eutectic high entropy alloy. This alloy exhibits an fcc + B2 (B2 with bcc nano-precipitates) microstructure resulting in a combination of the soft and ductile fcc phase together with hard B2 phase. Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength. The strengthening contribution due to fine scale L12 is modeled using Orowan dislocation bowing and by-pass mechanism. The alloy was tested under quasi-static (strain-rate = 10−3 s−1) tensile loading and dynamic (strain-rate = 103 s−1) compressive loading. Due to the fine lamellar microstructure with a large number of fcc-bcc interfaces, the alloy show relatively high flow-stresses, ~1400 MPa under quasi-static loading and in excess of 1800 MPa under dynamic loading.
